newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EMU reality may prove too much for Belgian OLOs.
newsitem.headline: EMU reality may prove too much for Belgian OLOs.

text.p: Belgian linear bonds (OLOs) have got another boost from Belgium's 1997 budget, presented on Tuesday, with 10-year benchmark yields now just a whisker over German levels.
But some OLO dealers believe the Belgian market's rise may not be taking into account the reality of life in an economic and monetary union (EMU) after 1999.
Ten-year OLOs, riding on the wave of EMU optimism that has gripped European markets all year, were Wednesday yielding 6.15 percent, a record low 12 basis points over equivalent Bunds.

"With this budget we are de facto members of EMU. We no longer need to realise this target, it has been achieved," a confident Belgian Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene told a news conference late on Tuesday.

Dealers universally agreed that in the near term the yield spread could narrow further to 10 basis points or less, a level undreamed of at the start of 1996, when the premium was at 70 basis points, or in 1990 - the year the OLO market was launched - when it was over 200.
"I can live with this level," Belgian central bank governor Alfons Verplaetse said in a newspaper interview last week.
Dealers said the market for now remained well supported by domestic demand, noting Belgium was the cheapest of the core European markets and also has the steepest yield curve.

But some said they believed a 10 basis point premium was too low, noting once exchange rates are locked on January 1, 1999, Belgium will no longer have any monetary policy leeway to cope with internal shocks that some believe are being stored up in the 1997 budget.
"People think that after EMU the spread will be 10 to 15 basis points, but that's not right. Once EMU happens the only way to punish countries is through their credit rating.
Therefore even after EMU the spread can go out to 30, one trader said.

"This budget like those of the last three years is full of temporary cuts and creative accounting. It does not tackle structural problems. After EMU, or even before, those are going to come out," he said.

Konrad Aigner of Deutsche Bank Research in Frankfurt said in the current euphoria over EMU, and with the yield pick up offered by Belgium over other core markets, a correct risk premium was hard to judge.
"I think it's between 10 and 30 basis points, 12 is a little bit too ambitious...It should be a touch higher," he said.

Others said such fears were overdone, noting the government's announcement on Tuesday that it wants to cut its deficit to 1.6 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) by 2000 from 2.9 percent of GDP in 1997 would, as Belgium's borrowing needs fell, be bond supportive.

Aigner said also that the downside risk for Belgium now seemed limited. "If the mood about EMU turns, the highest I can see is around 30 basis points...we will not now go back to the old levels of around 100 basis points," he said.
